title: Newton's Three Laws of Motion
hook: Three short rules — inertia, F=ma, and action-reaction — quietly govern almost everything that moves around you.
key_points: First law (inertia): an object keeps its velocity unless a net force acts on it.
Second law: net force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma.
Third law: for every force there's an equal and opposite force on the other body.
Together they let you predict motion once you know the forces involved.
content_html: Isaac Newton's three laws of motion, published in 1687, are the foundation of classical mechanics. The first law says objects resist changes to their motion — a property called inertia. The second law makes that quantitative: the net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration, written F = ma. The third law says forces always come in pairs: push on a wall and the wall pushes back on you just as hard.
extra_html: The power of these laws is that they turn "why does it move?" into a calculation. Add up all the forces on an object to get the net force; divide by mass to get acceleration; and acceleration tells you how the velocity changes over time. The same three rules describe a thrown ball, a braking car, and a planet orbiting the Sun. HyperPhysics walks through worked examples and the vector bookkeeping behind each law.

related.title: Mass vs. Weight
related.hook: Your mass is the same on the Moon as on Earth — but your weight isn't. They're related, but they are not the same thing.

related.title: Conservation of Energy
related.hook: Energy is never created or destroyed — it only changes form. That single rule is one of the most powerful ideas in all of physics.

related.title: Momentum: The Quantity of Motion
related.hook: A slow freight train and a fast bullet are both brutally hard to stop. Momentum captures why: it's mass times velocity, the real measure of moving 'oomph'.

flashcards.prompt: What does Newton's first law say about an object with no net force on it?
flashcards.back_html: It keeps its current velocity — staying at rest if still, or moving in a straight line at constant speed. This is inertia.

flashcards.prompt: Which equation states Newton's second law?

choices.text: F = ma (net force equals mass times acceleration)
F = mv (force equals mass times velocity)
F = m/a (force equals mass divided by acceleration)

flashcards.explanation_html: The second law links force to acceleration, not velocity: a bigger force, or a smaller mass, means more acceleration.

flashcards.prompt: A rocket pushes exhaust gas backward and is thrust forward. Which law is this?

choices.text: Third law — every force has an equal and opposite reaction force
First law — inertia keeps the rocket moving
Second law — force equals mass times acceleration

flashcards.explanation_html: The rocket pushes gas one way; the gas pushes the rocket the other way with equal force on a different body — the third law.
